title: Social Security’s Role in the Federal Debt Explosion
summary: Stronger wage growth improves Social Security’s finances, but it also raises future benefits because initial benefits are wage-indexed.
body_markdown:
The argument that Social Security has become a major contributor to the federal debt overlooks a fundamental feature of the program’s history: Social Security was established as a separately financed social insurance system, supported primarily by dedicated payroll contributions from workers and employers and governed by long-term actuarial principles. Social Security was never designed like ordinary federal expenditures such as national defense or other programs financed from general revenues. Workers and employers were specifically taxed to finance the system, eligibility was earned through covered employment, and benefits were tied to workers’ earnings records and insured status. Had the program been drafted as a general obligation program by Congress in 1935, it is doubtful it would have been passed. One cannot start by looking at the covered period from 2010 to the present. The original Social Security Act of 1935 created an Old-Age Reserve Account and specifically contemplated financing “on a reserve basis in accordance with accepted actuarial principles.” Funds not required for current benefits were to be invested in interest-bearing obligations of the United States. Congress formalized this structure in 1939 through the Federal Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund. This history matters because Social Security should not be analyzed simply as another federal expenditure whenever annual benefits exceed current payroll-tax receipts. Social Security benefits are not simply available to every American by virtue of citizenship. Workers earn insured status through covered employment—generally requiring 40 quarters of coverage for retirement benefits—and their earnings records help determine their benefits. Congress broadened the original retirement program in 1939 by adding benefits for spouses, dependent children and survivors, and later added disability protection. But these benefits generally remained connected to the earnings record and ensured status of the covered worker. A minor receiving survivor benefits, for example, may never have paid Social Security taxes, but the benefit exists because an insured parent did. Congress expanded what the worker’s Social Security insurance protected—from retirement alone to protection for the worker’s family against the economic consequences of retirement, disability and death. That is very different from an unrestricted general-fund entitlement. The Real Problem Is Failure to Maintain Actuarial Balance. None of this minimizes Social Security’s current financial problem. Dedicated revenues are insufficient to finance scheduled benefits indefinitely, and Congress must ultimately reconcile the difference through some combination of revenues, benefits, eligibility rules and retirement ages. But that is fundamentally an actuarial financing problem. Social Security was neither designed as a private investment account nor as an ordinary general-fund expenditure. It was designed as contributory social insurance, financed primarily through dedicated taxes and supported by trust funds intended to account for accumulated surpluses and future obligations. Congress established the benefits. Congress established the taxes. Congress expanded the program. Congress received continuing actuarial projections showing the developing imbalance. And Congress repeatedly decided whether to adjust revenues or benefits—or postpone doing so. The present shortfall therefore does not demonstrate that the original trust-fund concept was meaningless or that Social Security itself created the broader federal debt problem. It demonstrates the consequences of failing to maintain the financial balance of a system Congress was responsible for managing.
